title: 从 Ingress NGINX 迁到 Envoy Gateway，如何用加权 DNS 平滑切流
author: CNCF [Cloud Native Computing Foundation]
content:
Brief Description

Zero-Downtime Migration: From Ingress NGINX to Envoy Gateway with Weighted DNS - Andrew Katsikas

Table of Contents

  • Why migrate and what Gateway API changes
  • Controller selection and testing
  • Weighted DNS cutover and rollback
  • Production requirements and bootstrap deadlock
  • Upstream fixes and tenant policy
  • Migration takeaways
  • Questions about open source project selection

Why migrate and what Gateway API changes

All right. Thanks everybody for joining. My name is Andrew Katsikas. I'm the senior software engineer at PelaTech. We're a small um software engineering consulting firm specializing in Kubernetes and Cloud Solutions. Um and this talk is called the zero downtime migration from Ingress NGINX to envoy gateway with weighted DNS. Um so yeah, at PelaTech um I've had the opportunity to work on a wide array of um different projects for our clients and including this initiative uh to move them off of um the ingress API, specifically the Ingress NGINX controller and onto uh the new Kubernetes API, the gateway um using envoy gateway as the controller. Okay. So today what we're going to cover um we're going to talk a little bit about what the risks are for running Ingress NGINX today. Um so we'll talk about that.

We'll talk about the gateway API itself, the successor API to ingress. Choosing a controller, uh how that process went, what we evaluated, how we made a decision, um the actual zero downtime cutover technique using weighted DNS, some things we discovered in production, and um actually some upstream contributions to some great projects um including envoy gateway itself and uh the cert manager controller, which is also really nice. Okay. So the problem is that Ingress NGINX is end of life. Uh that happened in March of this year. Um so what does that mean? The contributors are done contributing. It's not um there are some successor commercial projects that have picked it up, I believe, but the sort of free open source model of Ingress NGINX is officially over. That means no new security patches, no new features, no development at all um to that original project um and so for people running Ingress NGINX, this kind of represents a supply chain liability.

So, any vulnerabilities discovered after this EOL aren't going to be patched. So that can that can be an issue specifically around like you know, there's there's actual risks like things that can happen, but I think beyond that just there's compliance exposure. So any unpatched infrastructure that you're running depending upon if you have to conform to like PCI DSS or HIPAA, that's an issue. And we've actually seen something specific with this not too long ago. It was this summer in June, there was the HTTP 2 bomb which affected a lot of different reverse proxies including Envoy, including NGINX. And you know, the actual data plane the control the actual reverse proxies did ship patches. So Envoy fixed it, NGINX fixed it. But Ingress NGINX doesn't get this update. So if you have this problem, you're only recourse rather than obviously migrating off of it is to patch it yourself and build your own image into the EOL codebase.

So kind of like forking it, which you know, is a lot of work. It's not as easy as just upgrading a version. So you know, this is a real problem. Additionally, just with ingress in general, there's sort of the annotation debt problem. Routing is exposed through these opaque unvalidated and controller specific annotations. And the API itself is feature frozen ingress itself. So there's not really any kind of exciting future for it. So let's talk a little bit about the replacement the gateway API. So this is where Kubernetes is heading. So before in ingress, you have one resource type. In gateway API, you have three resources kind of the gateway class where the infrastructure provider declares capabilities, the gateway where the cluster operator defines listeners and the HTTP route for instance, there's other kinds of routes, but that's where the application to team defines routing.

Um, for ingress, your routing is controlled through custom annotations, which are implementation specific and don't get validated. Um, and you cannot share these configurations across various controllers where with gateway you have typed resources, you get schema validation, and they tend to be pretty portable. There are some custom CRDs that are controller specific, but a lot of these kind of are if they're not already mainlined into the gateway API themselves, they're usually in like an experimental status. So the gateway API is evolving and more and more these kinds of resources get kind of applied across all sorts of controllers. So uh, that's a good option for portability and kind of a unified approach to the API, which is great. [clears throat] And here is just a little image from the official Kubernetes documentation.

Controller selection and testing

Um, you have your gateway class, which is your infrastructure providers are managing this, and then the cluster operators operate the gateway, and then application developers can you know work on their TLS routes, their HTTP routes for their services. So this is kind of the model. And you can kind of see the separation of concerns, whereas this used to kind of be all lumped together in one ingress resource, and it's now spread out. So it kind of respects the boundaries between teams with these different resources. So onto evaluating a controller, we evaluated five options. Envoy gateway, it met our mutual TLS needs and our buffering requirements. That was what we ended up selecting. We also looked at Istio. Um, we found that there was some complexity and awkwardness in the API. It didn't really fit with what we needed for the client.

We looked at Higress. It was not in the gateway API conformance results. Um, that's important to us. So, we were looking at those conformance results. We did not see them in there. So, um, we kind of passed that over. Uh, we did look at Traefik. It's a really good project, but it is kind of more of a commercially driven project where we're kind of um focusing on community supported options. And then we looked at NGINX Gateway Fabric, but that was outside of the um Cloud Native Computing Foundation filter that we sort of settled on. So, before we went to the customer with this, we tested on our own clusters. Um, if you've not used Kind, it's really great. That's Kubernetes in Docker. That's a disposable local cluster. Um, you know, you're not typically um doing load balancing when you're using Kind.

There are possibilities to do it, but otherwise it's a pretty highly realistic um environment that um is like a genuine Kubernetes cluster. We use this to compare options, uh map the ingress annotations to their HTTP route equivalents. Uh, we found a tool called ing-switch, that's probably stands for ingress, um on GitHub, which actually was able to scan our live cluster, kind of um inventory all of the resources on the cluster, take a look at any annotations they're using, and suggest gateway um API can uh compliant kind of equivalents. So, this took a lot of the work out of um planning for this migration, and then we were able to test those in Kind, um which is a really low stakes environment. It's It's really great for messing around, kind of experimenting and learning. So, we um were able to use that pretty effectively.

Um, once we felt that was working well, we ran on our own internal cluster, um so we could do full integration. So, we ran ingress and gateway API simultaneously with external DNS controller and cert manager. Um, additionally, it's important sometimes to install from scratch. Um, certain things um can come up with starting a cluster from the very beginning versus one that's live and already running. So we went ahead and tested on a uh brand new cluster. So this was the first time bootstrap with external DNS and cert manager building from zero. And this is where we found an issue um with a listener set deadlock. So really important to check that out. Kind of um this also kind of gives you a sense not only if a client or you know you are building a new cluster but also in kind of a disaster recovery scenario where you might need to start a brand new cluster.

Weighted DNS cutover and rollback

How is that going to work? So the cutover itself um you know moving traffic is fairly easy but dropping it with zero request is a little bit more difficult. Um when you swap A records you create a window where clients are resolving to the old TTL and they're going to be sending requests to a dead endpoint and you can't control that cache. Um and so weighted DNS is one solution we found to deal with this issue. Um you basically both the ingress um and the HTTP route running for gateway are registered under the same hostname. Um without weighted DNS typically you'd get like kind of a round robin uh type scenario where you're not really sure where traffic is going to go but with weighted DNS you can specifically say I want uh X percentage of traffic to go to the ingress versus the HTTP route.

Um and you shift the weight instead of deleting and creating records. Um once you feel that the cutover is successful that's when um you can delete the old records. And of course you create the new records first but you create them you can create them with zero weight so no traffic goes there. And then this provides a few benefits um in addition to not dropping any requests. Uh rollback if there's any issues is just two annotation changes. So it's a sort of non-disruptive way of accomplishing the cutover which is I think very helpful. Um so here's just a little picture into what the annotations look like. So the idea is shifting the weight and keeping both of the records. So in the initial state all traffic is on the ingress. Let's imagine that this annotation the top one commented ingress resource is of course the ingress resource and we say the weight for this is 100 whereas the HTTP route resource is a weight of zero.

So all traffic is going to flow to ingress and no traffic will flow to the HTTP route, but they both exist at the same time. Um you'll notice that for this is an AWS specific annotation but you know depending upon if you're using Google Cloud or Azure you should be able to find equivalence with external DNS. So external DNS is a custom Kubernetes controller we use for managing our DNS records and it has these provider specific annotations that allow you to do the weighted routing. And so you do this, you set these this up and then when you want to cut over you swap the weights. You shift the weights. You can also kind of think of it as like a hot swap. It's almost like that Indiana Jones thing where he's like taking the treasure and putting like a rock on it before it senses that he's stolen it.

It's a little bit like that. And in this case you swap the ingress over to zero and the HTTP route over to 100 and then your traffic is shifted without any downtime. The result was zero failed requests during the cutover. Yeah so you're running both of them in parallel. You're shifting the weight with Route 53 in our case AWS and external DNS and then the rollback is just reversing those annotations. We didn't have to do that, but it's nice to know that it's a very clean way of dealing with any problems and we I verified it with a shell script that continuously polled the new endpoint and saw that you know it was 200 through the entire of entirety of the cutover. So, I had that kind of tee up and both print out to the console and print out to a file and observe that there were no requests dropped during that time.

Production requirements and bootstrap deadlock

So, some [clears throat] of the production realities, what did internal testing surface? There was the need for mutual TLS with certificate forwarding. Production required that. Envoy gateway handles this natively. So, it was caught in annotation mapping and tested in kind, which was great. We also needed to enable request buffer limiting. The existing ingress config had buffer limits as annotations. Gateway API uses dedicated policy resources. We caught that in annotation mapping and tested in kind. And then finally, hostname duplication. So, with the gateway API, hostname definitions were duplicated actually at the gateway and HTTPRoute levels. But gateway 1.5 introduced the listener set concept, which allows for independent listener definitions. And so this is really good for single source of truth.

If you're using Helm charting, you can kind of define your hostname once and then have the Helm chart apply that hostname to both the HTTPRoute and the listener set. So, you do have kind of duplication, but it's defined once versus needing to define it in two different places with the gateway and the HTTPRoute. So, we found the listener set to be really useful for that. And we kind of figured that out when we were moving into production. Okay. So, we can talk a little bit about what we fixed and contributed back, some of the upstream contributions that I made to these various projects. And a lot of this really is around kind of listener sets and they're sort of being you know, kind of cutting edge at the time, maybe even still a little new. And finding some of the issues that kind of out with uh making use of listener sets and ensuring that um Envoy Gateway um could kind of um leverage them effectively and without bugs.

So this [clears throat] one was sort of a discovery between Envoy Gateway and Cert Manager. Um there was a listener set bootstrap deadlock. This was discovered during our fresh cluster test. So the scenario here is um you create a listener set which references uh TLS certificate that cert-manager hasn’t issued yet. So Envoy Gateway was setting its accepted false on the listener set. But that's really a bug. Um it should be accepted true and resolved references false. Um and I kind of looked at the um the gateway API spec itself to see if um it can kind of confirm my suspicion that it should work this way and it did make a strong suggestion that accepted um the accepted status is not really meant for um if the certification is present or not, but rather kind of like is the um listener set itself kind of well formed.

So the issue here is that external DNS is watching for accepted true on the listener set before creating its DNS records. Um and then without a DNS record, so external DNS is waiting to create that DNS record. And then Cert Manager cannot create a Cert without the DNS record. So I can't um we're using the ACME HTTP-01 challenge and it can't complete. So both of them are kind of waiting for one another to do something and neither of them want to proceed because this listener set is marked accepted false. So this is kind of a deadlock. So the certificate never gets issued because the DNS record never gets created and the DNS never gets issued because the Cert doesn't exist, right? So they're both in contention here and the listener set um stays as accepted false forever. So there's a fix and a feature that came out of this.

Upstream fixes and tenant policy

Um, so this is my first contribution to Envoy Gateway was to create a fix to set listener set accepted is true even if the um the certificate is invalid. It doesn't exist yet. So, again, the gateway API spec says that invalid certificate ref is a resolved refs problem, not an accepted status problem. So, we kind of reclassified the problem. Um, and now the listener set matches the gateway resources already worked like this. It was listener set because they're probably a little newer um weren't behaving the same way as the gateway. So, by fixing this, it kind of made the behavior more consistent between these two resources or identical really. Um, matched it more to the gateway API spec itself and fixed that deadlock issue or at least partially. We'll get more to that in a second. And so that got merged.

Additionally, there was a feature enhancement here around listener sets. So, with cert manager, um there was a PR I made to use the parent gateway as the HTTP 01 parent ref. Um, so for some users, listener sets are sort of TLS [snorts] only. Um, but the HTTP 01 solver needs an HTTP non secure listener to target um in order to make that challenge happen. So, there was a workaround. You can open up port 80 on every single listener set, but that's pretty arduous across tenants if you have a lot of different host names. Um, and so I thought why not just use the parent gateways um port 80 and then all of the children listener sets can then just use that and then your kind of cluster operator can set up the port 80 open on the gateway just once rather than for every single tenant. And then they can fall back to use that parent.

So, I created a new annotation for cert manager for that and that tells cert manager to use the gateway's port 80 for the purpose of the challenge. So this really cuts down on a lot of um repetitive configuration, which was useful. All right. So there's one more bug. This is called HTTP route status is not listener status. So here's the scenario. When an HTTP route is attached to a listener whose TLS cert wasn't ready, Envoy gateway was marking the route as accepted false. No ready listeners. But the route's binding is valid. The listener just wasn't programmed yet. So like the previous bug, controllers like external DNS need the positive accepted status. That's kind of like the base status, and it really should be reserved for configuration problems, not just the cert hasn't created yet. So if a route shows accepted false, external DNS doesn't create DNS records.

It's very similar to the last problem. Except instead of on the listener set, it's on the HTTP route. So there's another fix called separate listener program state from HTTP route accepted condition. And I removed the ready listener guard. And this also fixed TCP route and UDP route in addition to HTTP route. So similar concerns there. And with the gateway API, there's a three-layer status model. Accepted is the base. Is the route's binding to the listener valid? Then there's resolved refs. Can all of the referenced objects like certs and services be found? And then programmed. Is the listener's infrastructure ready to serve traffic? So accepted, we're kind of reserving for basic binding. So it's kind of like these different statuses and kind of tiers of statuses. And finally, I added a new feature to Envoy gateway for per-tenant policy control.

So previously, client traffic policy resource, which you know, you can set things like TLS version, timeouts, stuff like that, it could only target gateways. It could not target listener sets. And again, the platform team owns the gateway. The tenant owns listener sets. There was no per-tenant policy control. So that could pose a problem. The workaround was either to broadly applied the client traffic policy across the entire gateway for all listener sets attached, or drop the use of listener sets and rely on granular listens to listeners to find at the gateway level. So that kind of having to abandon this really nice new resource. Um, so instead I created a new feature which is to support listener sets as a target reference for client traffic policies. Uh, there's an important precedence that was established when I had did this PR which was that um you kind of um a policy targeting a specific section name wins is the most specific over a listener set wide policy and then finally a gateway wide policy.

So a platform team can define a client traffic policy at the gateway level, but it's going to be potentially overridden by something on a specific section name or listener set. So again that allows the platform team to set defaults while tenant teams can override at their listener set. So it's kind of like a nice cascading model here and the most specific policy should win. Uh, so in total there were four PRs across two projects. Um, there was the listener set accepted status bug fix, the first one that shipped in 1.8. Uh, there was another bug fix for the HTTPRoute status. That was 1.8.2. And then finally the feature which shipped in that minor version minor version revision 1.9 for the client traffic policy target listener sets. And the feature to cert manager for the parent fallback shipped in 1.21.

Migration takeaways

Uh, so there are a few takeaways from this presentation. Um, definitely evaluate against your specific production requirements. Tools like ing-switch really helped us identify that cuz you know you might not have like it's it's not necessarily easy if you have a lot of configurations to scan across your entire codebase. Um, you know it helps to have a working knowledge of what your infrastructure is doing, but you can also use automated tools to help you kind of inventory all your resources, uh get a sense of what you're running and using, and making sure that when you're selecting a controller that it's going to fit your specific production requirements. Additionally, you want to validate in a test environment before production. For us, this looked like using kind as the low stakes environment very early on.

Kind of once that was working, we moved on to our own internal cluster. Maybe you have a test cluster that you can run on. That's another good option. And then definitely consider if you can working on a totally fresh cluster cuz you know, if you ever need to spin up a fresh cluster for like a disaster recovery or a totally new environment, you want to make sure that whatever you're doing is going to work in that scenario as well. Um yeah, and so the weighted DNS was also a really nice technique that I think can be leveraged across different orgs. This ensures zero downtime. You shift the weights rather than having to delete resources. And that gives you the ability to have the effective zero downtime cutover. Definitely recommend contributing upstream when you find problems, gaps, bugs, new features that you need.

I found that agentic coding can be really helpful here and it helped me kind of get familiar with large code bases that I wasn't familiar with and kind of pinpoint where fixes and enhancements needed to be made. So I was definitely taking advantage of that and found that it helped with getting those features pushed in. And then staying current keeps your options open. So using the gateway API is going to you know, it's it's an API that's evolving, is getting feature updates. And whereas staying on ingress is going to kind of limit you because it's it's a feature frozen spec and it's not really going anywhere besides maybe bug fixes and things like that. So those are sort of the takeaways. Thanks for listening and I guess we'll do a Q&A now.

Questions about open source project selection

Host: Yeah. So if you have questions,

Guest: for Andrew, please use the Q&A at the bottom of the screen. There is a Q&A button that you can click. It sort of looks a bit like a chat. You can add questions there. But I think something that Andrew's done that is really exciting is that contributing back to the community when there are issues or challenges rather than just waiting for, you know, waiting for something to get done or being like, oh well, if that I think that's Is that one of the reasons why you chose to go with the community-driven project, Andrew, to be able to be involved in it?

Host: I don't think that I was expecting to be contributing to projects when I did the selection, but we definitely knew that with open source community-driven projects that if we found problems, we're much less likely to be sort of stuck. Um actually I guess that's something I didn't mention in the presentation, but um you know, part of the reason the ingress Nginx project uh I don't want to say fell apart. It sounds a little dramatic, right? But like there were like a couple of contributors working. Um and so actually one of the criteria I didn't mention this. I probably should have um we looked at the CNCF offers kind of a matrix of like health scores for various projects and Envoy Gateway had a lot of active contributors. They like to measure it not only how many active contributors are there, um how many companies do they represent?

So like a diversity of kind of or you know, a lot of different contributors is good. Um you know, an open community model. I was able to kind of just like join community meetings, get familiar with people, make those contributions and um you know, help the product for the greater community, but also to our specific needs. So I think yeah, choosing open community model is great because you kind of have that assurance even if you don't expect to contribute that if you need to and you need to get something fixed, that um you have a good chance of kind of affecting change in the project.

Guest: Yeah, you like you can unblock yourself in a way that if you have no ability and I think that helps school is so important as well because if there's very few maintainers or very few people then it can be really hard to even get your PR checked we know a lot of especially with the agentic coding though that has been an increasing PRs overall.

Host: Yeah, yeah, there's a lot of the maintainers to look at and yeah, like I was saying like Ingress NGINX I think there were like two guys um working on it at the end of uh the times and kind of we wanted to avoid that and so some of the other projects we looked at had like one person doing over 51% of the commits and it's like hm I don't really want to get back into that situation and then we find that this person has had enough of all the hard work and um you know all the free labor that we like tremendously benefit from and I think spreading that out among more people so burnout is less possible. You get more voices uh you just get a stronger product um a stronger project with more people involved I think.

Guest: We are sort of running out of time but you have a question in the Q&A that just in a moment ago.

Host: in the chat. Oh, so I should switch to

Host: Yeah, so you just got one I think if you can answer that offline we'll introduce Rohit and Rohit how do you pronounce your co-presenter's name?

Guest: It's Basundra.

Host: Basundra. I didn't want to butcher it so I left it due but yeah, thank you thank you Andrew and yeah, if you can answer that Q&A question in the Q&A that'll be amazing and we'll get Basundra on to the stage.

Guest: Yeah, regarding Traefik, so we actually that was one of the attractive things about it was that they are both they both offer a kind of for the same controller they offer an implementation and gateway API um and ingress so that actually was a pretty attractive option. It mostly was just down to them being a bit more of like a commercially oriented project that really um made us kind of like shy away from it. I didn't necessarily think it was like more of the same. I thought it's great that they offer both support for gateway and ingress and honestly is a really strong project and has a lot of good drop-in replacements if you choose to go the ingress route to switch off of ingress nginx. So I'd definitely recommend it as a strong project and worth a look for people. It just wasn't we felt like yeah it wasn't quite for us because of the community.

We were looking for something more community oriented but definitely a strong project.

Host: Thank you Andrew and I got your presentation now. Thank you so much.
aiSummary: Andrew Katsikas 介绍如何让两个端点并行运行，通过加权 DNS 从 Ingress NGINX 切到 Envoy Gateway，并把启动时遇到的问题反馈给上游项目。
oneSentenceSummary: Andrew Katsikas 介绍如何让两个端点并行运行，通过加权 DNS 从 Ingress NGINX 切到 Envoy Gateway，并把启动时遇到的问题反馈给上游项目。
summary: 这次迁移从选控制器、把 Ingress 注解映射到 Gateway API 资源开始，随后在本地、内部集群和全新集群演练。切换时两个端点都保留，只交换 DNS 权重。全新集群测试发现 ListenerSet 的接纳状态、ExternalDNS 建记录和证书签发之间可能互相等待。讲者用持续探测核对了本次切换结果，也说明了怎样撤回权重调整。

mainPoints.point: 按生产需求挑选控制器
mainPoints.explanation: 团队核对了双向 TLS、客户端证书转发、请求缓冲、可移植性和项目活跃度，并在不同测试环境里演练。

mainPoints.point: 保持两个端点在线再交换权重
mainPoints.explanation: 把两个端点注册在同一域名下，用 ExternalDNS 注解交换 Route 53 权重。需要回滚时，把注解改回去即可。
ExternalDNS 等 ListenerSet 被接纳，cert-manager 的 HTTP-01 验证却要先有 DNS。修复把绑定有效与就绪状态分开，也允许验证复用父级 Gateway 的监听器。

keyQuotes: 切换期间没有探测到失败请求。
两边都在等对方先做一步。
